[PAPER_0035, relevance_score=0.359] Similarly, the nature of the research question requires the use of a cross-sectional design to examine associations with age. We therefore cannot distinguish effects of chronological age from those related to cohort effects.

As preregistered at https://osf.io/tb4qv, we hypothesized that during the early-spring time bin, age would be positively associated with mental well-being (i.e., positively associated with positive mood and negatively associated with measures of depression, stress, worry, and negative mood).

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.329] These preregistered hypotheses were made prior to our knowledge of two other studies that had reported increased resilience of older adults during the pandemic (Klaiber et al., 2020; Varma et al., 2021). During the late-spring phase, once people would have had some time to adjust to the societal changes, and in the context of society "opening up" in a way that benefited younger adults more than older adults who were still urged to stay at home, we predicted that the advantage of age on mental well-being would decrease relative to the earlier time window.

[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.295] This hypothesis was tested against the alternative that the benefits related to older age would persist throughout both time windows assessed.

A secondary goal of the present study was to examine how exercise (operationalized as 20 min or more of daily activity) and perception of social isolation would affect mental health during these early and late-spring phases of the pandemic, and to examine whether the effects of these factors would differ as a function of age. Extensive research has shown that adults of all ages benefit from social interactions, with strong social networks tied to greater emotional well-being.

[PAPER_0039, relevance_score=0.201] Physical activity can also offset effects of stress (Sharon-David & Tenenbaum, 2017). Thus, we sought to examine how these factors would influence metrics of emotional well-being across the adult life span throughout the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. As preregistered, we hypothesized that age would be negatively associated with daily activity and with self-reported social connectedness, and that each of those factors would be positively associated with mental well-being.

[PAPER_0040, relevance_score=0.238] We further hypothesized that while the beneficial relation between age and mental well-being might dominate in the early-spring time window, by the final two weeks of the stay-home orders, exercise and social connectedness would be the primary drivers of effective coping.

[PAPER_0083, relevance_score=0.252] We found no evidence for our hypothesis that daily exercise would become a more important predictor of well-being in the later-spring phase. Broadly consistent with our hypothesis, but specific to the Worry Composite in a way we had not anticipated, a four-way interaction provided suggestive evidence that the combination of exercise and feelings of social connectedness enabled maintenance of the benefits conveyed by increased age from the first time point to the second time point.

A number of limitations should be noted when considering the generality of these results.

[PREREG_0008, relevance_score=0.417] Hypothesis: (1a) During the first two weeks of data collection (March 20-April 4, 2020), age will itself be positively associated with positive mood (as measured by the positive affect scale of the PANAS) and negatively associated with measures of depression, stress, and worry, and negative mood (as measured by the negative affect scale of the PANAS, modified PHQ-9 without the suicidality question, and COVID-related stress and worry questions), a prediction that is based on a large literature suggesting that adults become able to regulate negative emotions with age (Mather, 2012).

[PREREG_0009, relevance_score=0.348] This hypothesis will be tested against the alternate hypothesis that the benefits of age typically seen are reduced in the context of the stress of the COVID pandemic.

[PREREG_0010, relevance_score=0.217] (1b) During the final two weeks of wide spread stay at home orders (April 16-May 1, 2020), we expect that following the chronic threat and anxiety produced by COVID19, and in the context of society opening up more but in ways that benefit younger adults more than older adults who are still urged to stay home, the protective factors associated with age will become less apparent, such that age will show a lesser advantage to measures of mood, depression, stress, and worry than it did during the early weeks of the pandemic.

[PREREG_0011, relevance_score=0.418] This hypothesis will be tested against the alternative hypothesis that the benefits of age persist throughout the time of the stay-home orders and into these final weeks prior to reopening.

(2a) During both the early and later time windows, we expect age to be negatively associated with exercise and self-reported social connectedness, and each of these factors to be positively associated with mood. As noted in #1, we expect the effects of age to dominate in the first phase of data collection (Mar 20-Apr 4, 2020).

[PREREG_0012, relevance_score=0.236] However, by the final two weeks of wide spread stay at home orders (April 16-May 1, 2020), we predict that exercise and self-reported social connectedness will be the primary drivers of effective coping. Thus, if there are reduced effects of age on wellbeing in the final two weeks as compared to the first two weeks (Hypothesis 1b), this age x time interaction may be mediated by older adults' reduced exercise and reduced subjective experience of social connections during the pandemic.

[PREREG_0035, relevance_score=0.267] q22: As part of an exploratory analysis, we will also examine the impact of age on the complete sum of all worry questions as well as each of the worry questions separately to determine if COVID19 has had any age-related effects in other domains.

We will also investigate the utility of using questions of virtual socializing and encountering others "face-to-face" as measures of social connectedness, although we believe both questions have significant limitations. These variables will be log transformed before being used in regression models.

[PREREG_0036, relevance_score=0.259] These variables will be log transformed before being used in regression models. This reflects the expectation that these variables are more likely to have a logarithmic than linear relationship to mood outcomes-i.e., there will be a benefit of socializing and contact with people, but there will be diminishing returns to the benefit of these variables as the amount increase. In addition, the log transformation also reduces the significant positive skew and outliers in these variables. As such, our primary analyses are limited to their self-reported experience of social isolation/connectedness.

[PAPER_0041, relevance_score=0.491] Design and Methods

Participants

To recruit participants, emails were sent to all who had expressed an interest in being contacted about future studies being conducted by our research laboratory. Social media posts were also used to recruit participants, as were posts to listservs targeting those interested in cognitive psychology or related topics. In response to our call for participation, which we began to circulate on March 20, 2020, N = 1,920 participants from around the world completed the online informed consent to be enrolled in the study.

[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.379] Of this initial recruitment, n = 1,504 went on to complete an initial demographic survey, which enabled them to begin receiving the daily survey. All English-speaking adults over the age of 18 were invited to participate, regardless of preexisting medical or mental health diagnoses.

[PAPER_0043, relevance_score=0.400] Given that the spread of COVID-19 and time course of response measures differed by country, for the analyses here we focused only on respondents from the United States (n = 919) to reduce variability in the timeline of these events.1 The age of participants in this sample ranged from 18 to 89 years old (M = 36.8, SD = 15.7).

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.369] Daily Survey

To reduce participant burden, we utilized two versions of a daily survey (Short and Full Version), one of which was sent to the participants via e-mail each day of the assessment period following their enrollment. The Short Version included questions of subjective experience of stress, social engagement, exercise, step counts for participants with a previously owned pedometer (∼40% of sample), alcohol use, prosocial behavior, sleep, and experience of coronavirus symptoms and diagnosis status.

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.355] Exploratory Analyses With International Sample

While the goal of the present study was to determine the association of age with mental health outcomes during the onset of a pandemic and if it changed as response measures began to be relaxed, we explored whether the results identified here would persist with a larger, international sample, beyond the United States (as demonstrated in Varma et al., 2021). As such, we also conducted an exploratory analysis of Model 1 and Model 2 utilizing all participants who provided data during the assessed time period.

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.303] Importantly, the timeline for the surge of COVID-19 and response measures put in place differed substantially (e.g., earlier responses in China and Italy, no formal lockdowns during this time period in Sweden). As such, we removed the time bins from the model analyses and just looked at main effects of age from our entire international sample across the entire assessment period reported here. The main effects of age were replicated across the entire sample in both Model 1 and Model 2. Full results from these models can be found in

[PAPER_0094, relevance_score=0.425] Supplemental Tables 1-3  include the breakdown of participants by state/region, and a description of state-mandated lockdown and advisories issued during the time bins utilized for this study.

[PREREG_0017, relevance_score=0.424] After consenting, they provide their email address, which is the only identifiable information directly requested in the study. The email addresses are transferred to a password protected sheet on a secure BC server, and a unique and de-identified Subject ID is generated for each participant.

Participants are then sent an anonymous survey link through Redcap (a secure, password-protected web application for building and managing online surveys and databases) via email to complete the initial demographic form. Once the demographic form is complete, each participant receives the Full Version (see Variables tab for description) of the daily survey for three consecutive days.

[PREREG_0022, relevance_score=0.406] The compensation structure for the one-time surveys is also separate (see Compensation).

To maximize the security and confidentiality of each participant, entering their unique and de-identified Subject ID at the beginning of every survey is the only way to sync all of their data. These Subject IDs are not included in the open-access database (new IDs have been randomly generated). At the completion of the study, the data will be downloaded and stored on our secure BC database.

Demographic Survey

The demographic survey included reports of age, sex and gender, sexual orientation, race, socioeconomic status, marital status, military status, education, number of dependents, previous diagnoses of serious mental health and medical conditions, and the impact that COVID-19 has had on education and employment status. A draft view of the demographic survey used for all participants can be found here: https://bit.ly/BC-Demo.

[PAPER_0047, relevance_score=0.274] Daily Survey

To reduce participant burden, we utilized two versions of a daily survey (Short and Full Version), one of which was sent to the participants via e-mail each day of the assessment period following their enrollment. The Short Version included questions of subjective experience of stress, social engagement, exercise, step counts for participants with a previously owned pedometer (∼40% of sample), alcohol use, prosocial behavior, sleep, and experience of coronavirus symptoms and diagnosis status.

[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.313] For this report, we use the age reported on the demographic survey, the subjective experience of stress, and the self-reported exercise (daily activity) questions from the Short and Full Version of the daily surveys, as well as the PANAS positive scale, PANAS negative scale, worry questions (Worry Composite and individual health worry question), subjective social connectedness, and the modified PHQ-9 scale questions from the Full Version of the daily survey. The full data set has been made available for open access (Cunningham et al., in press).

It mean-centers continuous predictors and codes time as −0.5 and 0.5 [PAPER_0052] [PAPER_0053] [PAPER_0054] [PAPER_0055]. Exploratory analyses also use scores across the assessment period or collapsed across time bins [PAPER_0073] [PAPER_0096].

These averaged variables will be analyzed with a linear mixed model with a random intercept for subject. Each DV of interest will be analyzed in a separate model with age as a continuous predictor and time bin as a categorical predictor. For example, using syntax of lme4 R package:

stress ~ age*time_bin + (1|sub_id)

To test hypothesis 2, average self-reported social connectedness and proportion of days exercised within each time bin will be added to the model. For example:

stress ~ age*time_bin*exercise*social + (1|sub_id)

q18: We do not intend to transform any variable in our primary analyses, with the exception of linear transformations common in regression (e.g., centering a variable around the mean). We do plan to transform some variables in some exploratory analyses which we describe in detail below.

q21: When averaging across observations in each time bin, missing values will be ignored.

Linear mixed models naturally handle missing data, so no additional measures will be taken to deal with variables that are missing across all responses for a subject in a given time bin (i.e., missing values after averaging).

[PREREG_0035, relevance_score=0.287] q22: As part of an exploratory analysis, we will also examine the impact of age on the complete sum of all worry questions as well as each of the worry questions separately to determine if COVID19 has had any age-related effects in other domains.

We will also investigate the utility of using questions of virtual socializing and encountering others "face-to-face" as measures of social connectedness, although we believe both questions have significant limitations. These variables will be log transformed before being used in regression models.

[PREREG_0036, relevance_score=0.374] These variables will be log transformed before being used in regression models. This reflects the expectation that these variables are more likely to have a logarithmic than linear relationship to mood outcomes-i.e., there will be a benefit of socializing and contact with people, but there will be diminishing returns to the benefit of these variables as the amount increase. In addition, the log transformation also reduces the significant positive skew and outliers in these variables. As such, our primary analyses are limited to their self-reported experience of social isolation/connectedness.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.272] To assess overall worry, we created a Worry Composite by summing the responses to all worry questions on the daily surveys except for the worry question on individual health. Given the presentation of COVID-19, we expected worry about individual health to be impacted differently by age, and thus it was analyzed separately.

To test our hypotheses, we averaged across all responses for each participant in each time bin (early: March 20 - April 4; late: April 16 - May 1) for each variable. These averaged variables were analyzed with linear mixed models with a random intercept for subject.
